title: Lesson Plan — Quadratic Equations (Class 10 NIOS Mathematics)
subject: Mathematics
objectives: Recognise a quadratic equation in standard form a x^2 + b x + c = 0 and identify a, b, c.
Solve a quadratic equation by factorisation, by completing the square, and by the quadratic formula.
Compute the discriminant b^2 − 4 a c and use it to predict whether the roots are real-distinct, real-equal or non-real.
Use the relations α + β = −b/a and α β = c/a to verify roots or to construct a quadratic from given roots.
Translate a short word problem into a quadratic equation, solve it, and reject roots that contradict the situation.
prerequisites: Class 9 manipulation of linear equations and identities like (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2 a b + b^2.
Comfort with multiplying out brackets and combining like terms.
Familiarity with positive and negative integers and simple radicals (for D not a perfect square).
The zero-product property of real numbers.
materials: Whiteboard and markers (one colour reserved for the discriminant box)
A4 reference card listing the three solving methods, one per pair
Set of 'sort the equation' cards (linear vs quadratic vs higher-degree) for the Engage phase
Calculator (one per pair) for the speed–time word problem

activities.description: Sort-the-equation card warm-up: students receive 8 cards with equations such as 3 x + 4 = 0, x^2 = 25, x^3 − 1 = 0, x + 6/x = 5, (x − 2)(x + 5) = 0 and sort them into 'linear', 'quadratic' and 'neither'. Disagreement on the last two surfaces the idea that a quadratic is anything that *can be written* as a x^2 + b x + c = 0.
teacher_actions: Distribute cards; give 3 minutes for sorting.
Pick two pairs to share their 'tricky' cards.
Tease: 'Today we'll learn three ways to find x for the quadratic ones.'
student_actions: Sort cards with bench partner; flag any they disagree on.
Be ready to defend their classification in 1 sentence.

activities.description: Pair task: each pair gets the equation x^2 − 7 x + 12 = 0 and is asked to find ALL values of x that work, by trial. Most will spot x = 3 quickly; some will spot x = 4. The teacher then asks 'how do you KNOW there are no others?' to motivate the zero-product property and factorisation.
teacher_actions: Write x^2 − 7 x + 12 = 0 on the board.
Listen for trial-and-error strategies; record them.
Use the 'how do you know there are no others?' question to set up the Explain phase.
student_actions: Try integer values of x; discuss how to be exhaustive.
Note any pattern they spot in the factor pairs of 12.

activities.description: Direct instruction in three short blocks: (i) factorisation by splitting the middle term — derive the rule 'find two numbers with product a × c and sum b' and work x^2 − 7 x + 12 = 0 and 6 x^2 + x − 15 = 0; (ii) completing the square — derive the identity x^2 + 2 p x = (x + p)^2 − p^2 and run the six-step algorithm on x^2 − 6 x + 5 = 0; (iii) the quadratic formula — derive it once by completing the square on a x^2 + b x + c = 0, then apply it to 2 x^2 − 7 x + 3 = 0 and 3 x^2 − 6 x + 4 = 0. End with the discriminant table (D > 0 / = 0 / < 0) on the board.
teacher_actions: Build a 'three-method comparison' table on the board side-by-side.
Highlight the discriminant in a coloured box and revisit it after each example.
Have students predict whether each example will have 0, 1 or 2 real roots before solving.
student_actions: Take notes; replicate each worked example in their notebook.
Add the quadratic formula to a 'rules box' for quick reference.
Predict the sign of D before each example is solved.

activities.description: Application station: students work through six problems from the worksheet — two factorisations, one completing-the-square, one quadratic formula with non-perfect-square D, one discriminant classification, and one short word problem (rectangle with area 60 m^2). The teacher circulates and prompts students who get stuck to verbalise their first step.
teacher_actions: Circulate; offer the smallest hint that unblocks a student.
Collect common slips for the Evaluate discussion (sign errors on b, dropping ±, forgetting to reject negative dimensions).
Pair fast finishers with peers who need support.
student_actions: Solve the six problems individually, showing all steps.
Self-check the first three against the posted answer key.
Ask a peer before asking the teacher.

activities.description: Exit-ticket quiz: an 8-question MCQ + short-answer slip with at least one item per content area, drawn from the chapter's question bank. Students complete it silently in 9 minutes; the teacher then projects the answers and runs a 4-minute discussion focused on the two items most students missed.
teacher_actions: Distribute the exit-ticket; remind students it is individual work.
Time the quiz to 9 minutes strictly.
Quickly tally results and address the top two miss items.
student_actions: Self-mark and write a one-line reflection on any item they got wrong.

activities.description: Set homework: complete the rest of the worksheet, plus one CREATE-level prompt from the bank ('Construct a quadratic equation whose roots are 2 + √3 and 2 − √3, and verify by computing the discriminant'). Preview the next chapter (Arithmetic Progressions) by writing the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, … on the board and noting the constant difference.
teacher_actions: Announce homework due date and the CREATE prompt.
Bridge to the next chapter with the AP example.
student_actions: Pack the worksheet for home study.

homework: Complete the remaining problems on the Worksheet — Quadratic Equations handout.
Complete one CREATE-level prompt: construct a quadratic with roots 2 + √3 and 2 − √3, verify D = 12, and confirm the formula α + β = −b/a, α β = c/a.
Find a real-world quadratic (area, speed–time or projectile) from a newspaper, ad or textbook problem set, copy it in your notebook and solve it.
assessment_ideas: Use the 8-item exit ticket described in the Evaluate phase as a quick formative check.
Set a 12-question MCQ quiz drawn from the chapter's question bank for the next class as a summative assessment.
Mark one LONG_ANSWER problem (rectangle with area 60 m^2 OR train speed problem) using the auto-grade rubric.
Run a 5-minute peer-grading round on the CREATE homework using a two-criterion rubric (roots correct? discriminant correct?).
references: NIOS Secondary Mathematics, Module 1, Lesson 6: Quadratic Equations.
NCERT Class 10 Mathematics, Chapter 4: Quadratic Equations (for additional worked examples).
